τοῦ πατρός, καὶ μὴ ἐκπορευθῆναι, ὡς τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα· διά τε τὸ ἀποκλείεσθαι τὰς βλασφημίας αἱρετικῶν λεγόντων αὐτὸν κτίσμα καὶ υἱόν, ὥς ἐσμεν ἡμεῖς. καὶ τὸ ἅγιον δὲ πνεῦμα ἓν καὶ μόνον εἶναι γέγραπται, διά τε τὸ ἑνιαίως καὶ μόνως αὐτὸ ἐκ τῆς ὑποστάσεως τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς ἐκπορευθῆναι καὶ μὴ γεννηθῆναι, ὡς ὁ υἱός· διά τε τὸ μὴ κτίσμα, ὡς τὰ ἄλλα πνεύματα, ὑπονοεῖσθαι. 5.3 τὸ γὰρ ἓν οὐ δύο, οὔτε ἀλλότριόν ἐστι τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς οὐσίας πατρός, οὔτε διώρισται τῆς πρὸς τὸ ἓν ἑνώσεως· οὔτε πρὸς ἐκεῖνον ὕφεσιν ἔχει ἢ ἄλλον ἑαυτοῦ μᾶλλον συμφυέστερον ἢ ἀγχίθεον· οὔτ' ἀνέχεται ἢ ἀριθμὸς προσαγορεύεσθαι τῆς ἑνάδος οὐσίας ὂν ἢ τοῖς παρηγμένοις συντάττεσθαι, τῶν πάντα παραγαγόντων σὺν τῷ πατρὶ καὶ τῷ υἱῷ τυγχάνον. οὐ δύναται οὖν τὸ ἓν ἅγιον πνεῦμα οὔτε τῷ ἑνὶ πατρὶ ἢ τῷ ἑνὶ υἱῷ εἶναι ἀνόμοιον, οὔτε τῷ πλήθει τῶν πνευμάτων ὅμοιον. 5.4 καθάπερ γὰρ ἑνὸς ὄντος θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς καὶ ἑνὸς υἱοῦ ἀληθινοῦ πάντες οἱ κατ' εἰκόνα δι' ἀγαθότητα καὶ ἀφθονίαν αὐτοῦ ἐκλήθημεν θεοὶ καὶ υἱοί, –οὐκ ὄντες τῇ ἀληθεῖᾳ–κατὰ τό· «ἐγὼ εἶπα· θεοί ἐστε καὶ υἱοὶ ὑψίστου πάντες·» οὕτως ἑνὸς καὶ μόνου ὄντος ἁγίου πνεύματος ἀληθείας, πολλὰ πνεύματα λέγεται, οὐκ ὄντα τῇ φύσει πνεύματα τοῦ θεοῦ. 5.5 οὐ βλέποντες καὶ ἀνασκεπτόμενοι, ὅπως ἂν τοῖς θεολόγοις φαίνοιντο συμβαῖνόν τι λέγοντες, οὐκ ὀκνοῦσι καὶ ἄλλα ἐπιφέρειν βλαβερά. καὶ μοί, πρὶν ἅπαντος ἀκοῦσαι τοῦ λόγου, μέμψηται μηδὲ εἷς, εἰ βλάβην τὰ ἐκείνων καλῶ. εὑρήσει γάρ, ὅτι φθέγγονται, ἄντικρυς ἀντιπράττοντες τῇ γνώμῃ τῶν θεηγόρων ἀνδρῶν, οἳ τὸ περὶ τοῦτο διαπρέπειν εἶχον παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν δωρεᾶς μέρει. λέγουσι γάρ· εἰ θεὸς τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα ἢ πατὴρ ἢ υἱός ἐστιν· μὴ ὂν δὲ τούτων μηδέν, οὔκ ἐστι θεός, ὡς οὐδὲ τὰ ἄλλα πνεύματα. 5.6 ἀπαντητέον τοίνυν αὐτοῖς 51 οὑτωσί, ὥσπερ θεὸς ὁ πατὴρ οὐ διὰ τὸ εἶναι πατέρα, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ εἶναι θείας φύσεως, καὶ ὁ υἱὸς οὐ διὰ τὸ εἶναι τοῦ τυχόντος υἱόν, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ εἶναι υἱὸν λόγον καὶ ἀναγκαίως τῆς αὐτοῦ θείας φύσεως ὑπάρχειν, οὕτως καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα θεὸς οὐ διὰ τὸ ἁπλῶς εἶναι πνεῦμα, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ εἶναι ἓν καὶ μόνον πνεῦμα ἅγιον, καὶ τῆς αὐτοῦ θείας φύσεως καθεστάναι, ὡς προελέχθη. καὶ ὥσπερ ἀκούσαντες· «εἷς ὁ θεός» καί· «κυρίῳ τῷ θεῷ σου προσκυνήσεις, καὶ αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις·» ἐξ ἴσου τῷ πατρὶ θεόν τε εἶναι τὸν μονογενῆ λόγον πιστεύομεν καὶ προσκυνοῦμεν καὶ λατρεύομεν αὐτῷ· τὸν ἴσον τρόπον καὶ περὶ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος διακείμεθα. 5.7 αὐτῷ γάρ, ᾧ προσετάχθημεν ἐν τῷ περὶ τοῦ ἀφθάρτου βαπτίσματος δοθέντι ὅρῳ, ἐξ οὗ ἤρτηται ἡ τῆς πάσης ἡμῶν πολιτείας καὶ θρησκείας κατάστασις, συντάττειν αὐτὸ τῷ πατρὶ καὶ τῷ υἱῷ προσετάχθημεν καὶ συμπροσκυνεῖν καὶ συνδοξάζειν αὐτὸ καὶ λειτουργεῖν αὐτῷ. αὕτη γάρ ἐστιν ἡ λογικὴ λατρεία, ἢν ἔγραψεν Παῦλος τοιῶσδε· «ἵνα παραστήσητε τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν θυσίαν ζῶσαν, ἁγίαν, εὐ άρεστον τῷ θεῷ τὴν λογικὴν λατρείαν.» 5.8 καὶ ὃν τρόπον, τοῦ ἀποστόλου τὸν θεὸν μόνον σοφόν τε καὶ ἔχειν ἀθανασίαν χρησμῳδήσαντος, πιστεύομεν καὶ τὸν υἱὸν ὁμοίως ἔχειν ἀθανασίαν καὶ εἶναι σοφόν, ἅτε ἀπαράλλακτον κατ' οὐσίαν ὄντα τῷ πατρὶ καὶ λόγον αὐτοῦ καὶ ζωὴν αἰώνιον, ὡς γράφει, ὑπάρχοντα· οὕτως καὶ περὶ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος. οὐ γὰρ κατὰ χάριν ἤτοι δόσιν ἔχει ἀθανασίαν καὶ σοφίαν, ὁμοίως τῶν λειτουργικῶν πνευμάτων, ἀλλὰ φύσει κέκτηται· πνεῦμα γὰρ σοφίας ἐστίν. τοιγαροῦν γέγραπται, ὡς· «οὐδεὶς γινώσκει τὰ τοῦ μόνου σοφοῦ, εἰ μὴ τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ.» εἰ γὰρ δοίησαν μὴ ταῦτα οὕτως ἔχειν, ἢ παρακρούσονται τὸν θεὸν
pass_a_gloss: [Continuing from the previous section, where the heretics argue: 'For if he were, he would not have been called only-begotten, but the] Holy Spirit would have been called his brother.' 5.2 Those men [speak] thus, being unlike even to themselves, but the truth [speaks] to them. He is written 'only-begotten' both because of his alone having been begotten from the hypostasis of the Father and not having proceeded, as the Holy Spirit [did]; and because of the shutting out of the blasphemies of heretics saying he is a creature and a son, as we are. And the Holy Spirit too is written to be one and only, both because of its having proceeded singly and solely from the hypostasis of the God and Father and not having been begotten, as the Son [was]; and because of its not being suspected [to be] a creature, as the other spirits [are]. 5.3 For the one [is] not two; neither is the Spirit foreign to the essence of the Father, nor has it been separated from the union toward the One; nor does it have a falling-short toward that one, or another more connatural or nearer to God than itself; nor does it endure either to be called a number, being of the essence of the Unity, or to be ranked with the things brought forth, being one of those who brought forth all things with the Father and the Son. So the one Holy Spirit can be neither unlike the one Father or the one Son, nor like the multitude of the spirits. 5.4 For just as, there being one God and Father and one true Son, all of us who are after the image were called gods and sons through his goodness and lack of grudging, not being [so] in truth, according to: 'I said, you are gods and sons of the Most High, all of you'; so, there being one and only Holy Spirit of truth, many spirits are spoken of, not being by nature spirits of God. 5.5 Not seeing and examining how they might appear to the theologians to be saying something consistent, they do not shrink from bringing in other harmful things too. And let not even one person blame me, before hearing the whole argument, if I call their [views] harm. For he will find that they utter [things], directly acting against the mind of the God-speaking men, who had from God, by way of a gift, the excelling in this. For they say: if the Holy Spirit is God, it is either Father or Son; but being none of these, it is not God, as neither [are] the other spirits. 5.6 One must answer them therefore thus [a printed page number 51 stands here in the copy-text]: just as the Father [is] God not because of his being Father, but because of his being of divine nature, and the Son not because of being son of anyone at all, but because of being the Son, the Word, of God and necessarily being of his divine nature, so also the Holy Spirit [is] God not because of simply being a spirit, but because of being the one and only Holy Spirit of God, and being established of his divine nature, as was said before. And just as, having heard 'God is one' and 'You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone', we believe the only-begotten Word to be God equally with the Father, and we worship and serve him; in the same manner we are disposed also about the Holy Spirit. 5.7 For him, whom we were commanded in the rule given about the incorruptible baptism, on which hangs the settled order of our whole way of life and worship, we were commanded to rank with the Father and the Son, and to worship together and glorify together, and to serve him. For this is the reasonable worship, which Paul wrote thus: 'that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, well-pleasing to God, the reasonable worship.' 5.8 And in the manner that, the apostle having declared God alone both wise and having immortality, we believe the Son likewise to have immortality and to be wise, inasmuch as he is indistinguishable in essence from the Father and is his Word and eternal life, as it writes; so also about the Holy Spirit. For it does not have immortality and wisdom by grace or gift, like the ministering spirits, but possesses [them] by nature; for it is Spirit of wisdom. Therefore it is written that: 'no one knows the things of the only wise one, except his Spirit.' For if they should grant that these things are not so, either they will defraud the God [continues in the next section: 'Word, or they will seem to act against the Scriptures'] ...
pass_b_english: …Holy Spirit would have been called his brother.”

So they argue, out of tune even with themselves; but the truth answers them. The Son is written “only-begotten” both because he alone was begotten from the hypostasis of the Father, and did not proceed, as the Holy Spirit does; and so that the blasphemies of heretics who call him a creature, and a son in the way we are sons, may be shut out. The Holy Spirit, too, is written to be one and only, both because he alone, in a single way, proceeded from the hypostasis of God the Father and was not begotten, as the Son was; and so that he may not be suspected of being a creature, as the other spirits are.

For the one is not two. The Spirit is not foreign to the Father’s essence, nor is he cut off from union with the One. He does not fall short of the Father, nor is there anyone more one in nature with him, or nearer to God, than the Spirit himself. Nor does he allow himself to be called a number, since he belongs to the essence of the Unity, or to be ranked with the things that were brought into being, for he is one of those who brought all things into being, with the Father and the Son. The one Holy Spirit, then, cannot be unlike the one Father or the one Son, nor like the multitude of spirits.

For while there is one God and Father, and one true Son, all of us who were made after the image have been called gods and sons through his goodness and generosity, though we are not so in truth, as the words run: “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Psalm 82:6). Just so, while there is one and only Holy Spirit of truth, many spirits are spoken of that are not by nature spirits of God.

Without stopping to look and consider how they might seem to the theologians to be saying anything consistent, they do not hesitate to bring in other harmful notions as well. And let no one blame me, before he has heard the whole argument, if I call their views harm. For he will find that what they utter runs straight against the mind of the men who spoke of God, men who received from God, as a gift, the power to excel in this very matter. For they say: “If the Holy Spirit is God, he is either Father or Son. But since he is neither of these, he is not God, any more than the other spirits are.”

We must answer them in this way. The Father is God not because he is Father, but because he is of the divine nature. The Son is God not because he is the son of just anyone, but because he is the Son and Word of God and is necessarily of his divine nature. Just so, the Holy Spirit is God not because he is simply a spirit, but because he is the one and only Holy Spirit of God and stands in his divine nature, as was said before. And though we have heard “God is one” (Romans 3:30) and “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve” (Matthew 4:10), we still believe that the only-begotten Word is God equally with the Father, and we worship him and serve him. In the same way we stand toward the Holy Spirit.

For in the rule given about incorruptible baptism, on which the whole order of our life and worship hangs, we were commanded to rank him with the Father and the Son, to worship and glorify him together with them, and to serve him (Matthew 28:19). This is the reasonable worship of which Paul wrote: “that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, well-pleasing to God, your reasonable worship” (Romans 12:1).

And though the Apostle declared that God alone is wise (Romans 16:27) and has immortality (1 Timothy 6:16), we believe that the Son likewise has immortality and is wise, since he is indistinguishable from the Father in essence, and is his Word and eternal life, as Scripture writes. So too with the Holy Spirit. He does not have immortality and wisdom by grace or by gift, as the ministering spirits do; he possesses them by nature, for he is the Spirit of wisdom. That is why it is written: “No one knows the things of the only wise One except his Spirit” (1 Corinthians 2:11). For if they should grant that these things are not so, they will either defraud God …

choices.issue: Garbled machine draft, wrong references, filler bracket
choices.choice: 2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-e-u13): retranslated from the Greek. The old English read 'the Apostle, having prophesied that the Son alone is both wise and possesses immortality' (Greek: God alone), 'may I, before hearing the whole word, be rebuked if not even one of them is found to harm their good' (Greek: let no one blame me if I call their views harm), 'the truth is toward them', 'as was foreordained' (προελέχθη, said before), 'the Son of God the Word' and 'being unchangeable in essence'; it split the heretics' syllogism of 5.5 across two paragraphs ('if God the Holy... / A Spirit is either Father or Son'). References: (Deut 6:4) -> (Romans 3:30); (Deut 6:13) -> (Matthew 4:10); (Rom 12:1) and (1 Cor 2:11) written out; (Matthew 28:19), (Romans 16:27), (1 Timothy 6:16) added. Bracket '[gods]' removed.

choices.english: …Holy Spirit would have been called his brother.”
choices.why: The section opens inside the heretics' quoted objection (5.1, previous section: 'if he were, he would not have been called only-begotten, and the Holy Spirit would have been called his brother'). Only the words this section holds are translated, opened with '…'; the potential sense ('would have been') carries over from ἂν in the previous clause.
Elliptical: a verb of speaking is understood, matching 'those men [speak] thus'.

choices.english: a son in the way we are sons
choices.why: The heretics make the Son a son by adoption like us; 'only-begotten' rules that out.
Kept literal: the Spirit, being of the essence of the Unity, is not an added unit in a count of beings.

choices.english: all of us who were made after the image
choices.why: Genesis 1:26 language for human beings; 'made' is needed in English for the elliptical phrase.

choices.english: the theologians / the men who spoke of God
choices.why: Both words mean the inspired writers of Scripture, not later church teachers.

choices.english: We must answer them in this way.
choices.why: 51 is a printed page number in the copy-text, skipped.
A word split by the copy-text's line break; read as εὐάρεστον.

choices.english: For in the rule given about incorruptible baptism ... we were commanded to rank him
choices.why: The Greek repeats 'we were commanded' after a long relative clause (anacoluthon); the English states it once. The rule of baptism is Matthew 28:19, which Didymus names this way elsewhere (u16-rem-early).
Didymus himself says in 5.10 that Paul wrote εἷς ὁ θεός to the Romans, Galatians and Timothy; Romans 3:30 has the exact wording. Deuteronomy 6:4 (the old reference) reads differently.
Didymus' words are the Gospel form (Matthew 4:10, Luke 4:8); Deuteronomy 6:13 LXX has φοβηθήσῃ, 'fear'.

choices.term: «οὐδεὶς γινώσκει τὰ τοῦ μόνου σοφοῦ, εἰ μὴ τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ»
choices.why: Didymus adapts 1 Corinthians 2:11, putting 'the only wise One' (Romans 16:27) for 'God'; the verse is the one he quotes.

The sentence runs into the next section (λόγον, 'the Word'): they would rob God the Word of the wisdom and immortality that are his by nature. Only the words this section holds are translated, ending with '…'.
